title: Noisy-tenant spectra hunt - notes & prototype throttle blueprint
content:
Summary:

This is a working log & runbook prototype for investigating noisy-tenant spectral signals (intermittent throughput/latency degradation) observed in a subset of dedicated GPU pools over 2025-11-22 -> 2025-11-24 (holiday weekend). Unlike previous 'burst' incidents this one presented as long-tailed latency for midsize requests and progressive eviction cascades in select nodes. Notes below capture the hunt, quick mitigations, an experimental adaptive throttle idea, and next steps.

Context / why this matters:
- Customers on Dedicated saw increased 95th/99th token latency for generation routes (seq len ~512). Impact was sporadic: some tenants fine, others repeatedly hit transient slowdowns and evictions.
- Autoscaler did not add healthy capacity despite queue growth; eviction churn increased and led to degraded throughput for ~3 hours on the worst-affected shard.
- Root-level hypothesis: a combination of a noisy tenant (amplifying KV cache churn) + an autoscaler hysteresis misconfig that delayed scale-up + affinity packing causing hot nodes.

Raw timeline (compressed):
- 2025-11-22 02:10 UTC: First spike in 99th latency alerted (route: /v1/generate-dedicated).
- 02:12: Pager oncall paged, initial triage -> saw 15% increase in eviction ops on pool-ff-04.
- 02:25: Identified tenant X with bursty long-history requests; producer profile shows many partial-prefix changes (likely streaming-style gen + re-rolls).
- 02:40: Autoscaler logs show scale decision suppressed due to hysteresis window; target nodes queued but cooldown prevented immediate allocation.
- 03:05: Manual temporary mitigation applied: soft-rate-limit on tenant X via token bucket (set r=10 req/min, burst 4) — immediate 20–30% reduction in evictions observed.
- 04:00: Traffic pattern moved to other nodes; observed repeated cache miss amplification in KV eviction metric.
- 05:30: Autoscaler cooldown adjusted and two extra nodes brought up; latency returned to near baseline by 06:10.

Investigation notes (what we looked at):
- Metrics correlated: per-tenant KV-cache-miss-rate, per-node GPU-utilization, per-node eviction_count, scheduler affinity churn, and autoscaler_decision_latency.
- Heap of evidence points to tenant request shapes that cause frequent new KV keys (small prefixes, many distinct prompt prefixes) causing LRU churn and large memory copy ops. That increases inference time jitter and can push node into eviction.
- Affinity packing ensured tenant co-located with others on same nodes -> noisy neighbor amplification.
- Autoscaler behavior: hysteresis uses 10-min cooldown by default; scale-up suppression rule did not recognize sustained 5-min elevated queue depth with high eviction_count as a trigger.

Quick mitigations taken (and rationale):
- Soft per-tenant rate limit (token-bucket) on the noisy tenant - cheap and effective to stop immediate eviction cascade.
- Temporary affinity soft-anti-affinity moved tenant off the hottest nodes (manual scheduler hint) - reduced tail latency for co-tenants.
- Manual autoscaler cooldown override to force upscaling - resolved capacity shortage while we stabilized mechanisms.

Runbook draft (steps for oncall when similar alarm occurs):
1) Observe alarm: route + pool + node list -> collect top-5 tenants by KV-cache-miss-rate and request-rate.
2) If top tenant(s) show >X KV misses/sec and eviction_count rising: apply temp soft rate limit (token bucket: r=xx burst=yy) and note ticket.
3) Apply scheduler hint: set soft-anti-affinity for top noisy tenant to redistribute.
4) Check autoscaler_decision_latency and cooldown state; if scale-up is suppressed and average queue depth > Q_THRESHOLD for 5m, escalate to manual cooldown override.
5) If after 10 minutes tail latency not improved, run node-level diagnost tools (collect debug heap, nvml stats, kernel logs) and snapshot KV cache keys for sampling.
6) Revert limits and affinity only when metrics stable for 20m and eviction_count trending to baseline.

Open hypotheses / unresolved questions:
- Why does this tenant produce such high KV churn? Two possibilities: (a) client uses frequent small-perturbation prompts that bust prefix reuse, (b) client-side library is spinning many near-duplicate requests. Need request-level traces.
- Is our KV cache eviction policy too aggressive for mixed tenant workloads with long-tail prefixes? Could consider TTL-based decay for rarely-hit keys.
- Autoscaler suppression rule probably needs a new predicate that considers eviction_count and sustained queue depth together.

Experiment log (what we tried in the moment):
- Soft-per-tenant throttling: (r=10/s, burst=30) reduced instantaneous evictions by ~35% within 5m. Too harsh for some customer flows; made it a short-lived mitigation and informed SRE to contact account team.
- Soft-anti-affinity: scheduler hint API used to move pods away; nodes rebalanced and GPU-utilization smoothed. There was a small spike in cold-start latency for moved instances.
- Autoscaler override: forced allocation of 2 nodes reduced queue depth and evictions; confirmed autoscaler cooldown gating is too conservative for eviction scenarios.

Prototype idea: Adaptive spectral throttle (sketch)
- Concept: lightweight per-tenant spectral fingerprinting (short sliding window histogram over request prefix-hash diversity + average KV cache miss ratio). Compute a 'spectral-noise' score (0..1).
- If score > 0.7 and eviction_count on node > threshold, apply graduated throttle: reduce concurrency first (soft), then ingress rate. The throttle decays automatically as score drops.
- Rationale: less manual intervention, acts before autoscaler cooldown becomes critical, and isolates noisy tenants without hard eviction-driven failures.
- Data needed: evaluation on historical traces for false positive rate; gauge customer UX; simulate with small subset of tenants on gamma-pool.

Immediate action items (who / by when):
- (Priya) Draft quick autoscaler rule patch: add eviction_count predicate to scale decision within 72 hours. -> JIRA DED-2347.
- (Liam) Build small gamma-pool experiment to run prototype spectral scoring on 5 known noisy tenants (start by 2025-11-30).
- (Aisha) Coordinate with solutions-engineering to notify affected account and prepare rollback plan for any customer-visible throttles (today).
- (Diego) Capture request-level traces from tenant X (sampling) and upload to S3 for analysis (by 2025-11-25).

Postmortem notes (short):
- Root cause (probable): A high-diversity request pattern from tenant X caused KV cache churn + affinity packing created noisy neighbor effect. Autoscaler cooldown and suppression rules delayed capacity add.
- Contributing factors: lack of a metric predicate for eviction-driven scale-up, absence of auto-synthesized per-tenant throttle, and affinity packing aggressiveness.

Communication plan:
- Internal: share this doc in #sre-oncall and link to JIRA DED-2345/2347.
- Customer: CS to send brief incident note with timeline + compensating actions; include note that we applied temporary rate limit (explicit permission path for any future auto-throttle).

Notes to follow up during post-incident review:
- Simulate workload in staging to benchmark spectral-score false positives.
- Consider KV cache policy changes: TTL decay vs LRU tuning; measure cost/benefit.
- Autoscaler: design an emergency bypass predicate for eviction-driven scenarios; shorten effective cooldown for scale-up when eviction_count>HIGH.

Scratchpad / quick commands used during hunt (for oncall reference):
- curl api/metrics?pool=pool-ff-04&metric=kv_miss_rate
- allocate-scheduler-hint --pool pool-ff-04 --tenant tenant-X --soft-anti-affinity
- override-autoscaler --pool pool-ff-04 --reason "eviction-churn" --force-scale 2

Random notes / TODOs:
- Check NVML logs for GPU PCIe errors (low confidence link).
- Add cross-team review with serving-runtime to see whether model execution patterns can be optimized for repeated small prefix runs.

If you are reading this oncall: please add anything you tried in the 'experiment log' section. This is intentionally a rough working doc; we will formalize into a shorter runbook once we validate the spectral scoring behavior.

-- Priya (oncall SRE)
